The world, for Elara, was circumscribed by the scent of old paper and leather binding. Her uncle, Mr. Alistair Finch, was its quiet, presiding sovereign, a man whose passions were for calfskin folios and whose sorrows were indexed upon the shelves of his own heart. He sat now in his accustomed chair, a pool of lamplight silvering his thinning hair, his finger tracing the marbled pattern on the endpaper of a book he was not reading.

“The account he kept was a curious one,” Mr. Finch said, his voice a low murmur that seemed another part of the shop’s deep quiet. “He recorded not what he earned, but what he owed; not in sums of money, but in small kindnesses he felt he had failed to repay. A strange ledger for a man of business.”

“Was he a friend of yours, Uncle?” Elara asked, her own needle pausing over the stocking she was darning. She looked at him, her gaze as clear and steady as his was distant.

“He was my brother, child. Your father.” He spoke the words as if they were a confession long rehearsed. “You have his eyes, you know. But not his restlessness. His spirit was a flickering candle in a constant draught; yours is a steady lamp. Can you understand such a distinction, Elara? Perhaps not. I pray you never have cause to.”

Before she could frame a reply, the door to the shop flew open with a violence that set the little bell above it into a frantic, protesting jangle. Mrs. Gable, their housekeeper and the sworn enemy of all dust and sentiment, stood upon the threshold, her bonnet askew.

“A fine thing, filling a girl’s head with ghosts and ledgers before breakfast!” she declared, her voice as brisk as the March wind she had admitted. “There is a young man at the door, Alistair, who will not be put off. He has a name like a churchyard stone and the patience of a bailiff.”

“And what name is that, Mrs. Gable?” Mr. Finch asked, his calm manner a stark contrast to the housekeeper’s flustered state.

“He calls himself Croft,” she announced, as if the name itself were an impertinence. “And he asks for you, by the title of your old firm; the one you do not speak of.”

Elara watched as a change passed over her uncle’s face. It was not a grand or sudden thing, but a quiet drawing-in of his features, a shuttering of the gentle light in his eyes, as though a familiar dread, long kept at bay, had just knocked upon the door of his soul. He rose from his chair, placing the unread book upon the table with a hand that was suddenly, minutely, unsteady.

“Show him into the study, if you please, Mrs. Gable,” he said, his voice now devoid of all its former warmth. “Elara, my dear, perhaps you might see if Mrs. Gable requires any help with the tea.”

The young man who entered was tall and grave, his face possessing a kind of stern handsomeness that seemed to Elara to have been carved by some sorrow. He gave a short, formal bow to Mr. Finch, his eyes passing over Elara with a glance of cool, assessing curiosity that made her feel, for the first time, like a stranger in her own home.

“Mr. Finch,” the young man said, his tone respectful but firm. “My name is Silas Croft. My late father was Jeremiah Croft.”

The name meant nothing to Elara; it meant everything, it seemed, to her uncle. She had never seen her uncle’s face so devoid of its customary scholarly warmth; it was a mask of courteous stone, and a deep-worn track of some ancient pain seemed to reappear around his mouth, a track she had never noticed before.

“I see,” was all Mr. Finch said, though his quiet tone was heavier than any shout. “We will speak in my study.”

He did not look at Elara as he passed her, but laid a cold hand briefly on her shoulder, a gesture that was meant to be reassuring, but which chilled her to the bone. The two men disappeared into the small back room, the one reserved for the rarest books and the most private accounts, and the door closed behind them with a soft, final click. And Elara, left alone in the sudden gloom of the shop, felt a coldness creep into the air that had nothing to do with the morning, and everything to do with the closing of that door.

It was the face of the prisoner from the Bastille. The intelligence, the warmth, the serene wisdom of the past years had been wiped away as if they had never been. His eyes were vacant, clouded, and unseeing. They looked upon Mr. Lorry and Miss Pross with no flicker of recognition, seeing only a disturbance, an interruption of his task. Miss Pross, with her customary and bracing lack of sentimentality, was the only one who partook of the meal with any genuine appetite; though even she, casting a sharp eye from Lucie’s pale cheeks to Darnay’s untouched plate, remarked that one would think a funeral, and not a wedding, had just been celebrated. “And if you are going to waste good food,” she declared, aiming her fork at Darnay’s toast, “then there are those of us with a stronger constitution who will not see it perish.”

“I beg your pardon, Miss Pross,” Charles said, attempting a smile that did not reach his eyes. “My thoughts were elsewhere.”

“They have been elsewhere since the middle of the night, I should venture,” she retorted, though with less asperity than usual; for she, too, had heard the floorboards creak, and had seen the line of light under the drawing-room door.

It was Mr. Lorry who brought the world, and all its attendant troubles, to their door that morning. He arrived near ten o’clock, his face a mixture of business-like gravity and personal concern. He carried a small packet of letters, as was his custom when he came from Tellson’s, but there was one letter that he held separate from the others. It was thin, the paper creased and of a poor quality, the address scrawled in a desperate hand and blotted in several places. It bore the postmark of Paris.

“A dispatch for Mr. Darnay,” he announced, holding it out. “It came by the last packet, addressed to him, care of Tellson’s Bank, London. It seems a matter of some urgency.”

A silence fell upon the room. The letter lay in Mr. Lorry’s hand, not a mere piece of folded paper, but an emissary from that other world, the dark and churning sea of revolution from which they had all, they thought, found a safe harbour. Charles looked at it as a man might look upon a warrant for his own arrest. Lucie involuntarily put her hand upon his arm, as if to hold him back from the precipice it represented.

He took the letter. His fingers, as he broke the crude wax seal, were perfectly steady. The stillness in the room was so absolute that the crackle of the unfolding paper sounded like a rending of the fabric of their peace. As his eyes scanned the lines of frantic, sloping script, what little colour had been in his face drained away, leaving it a mask of pale resolution. He read it through once; then, as if disbelieving, he read it through a second time.

“Charles?” whispered Lucie, her voice fraught with a fear she could no longer conceal. “What is it? What dreadful news?”

He looked at her, and in his eyes she saw not only sorrow, but a profound and weary pity, as if he were already looking at her from a great distance. “It is a summons,” he said, his voice quiet but carrying the weight of a final judgment. “From a man who is in mortal peril on my account.”

“On your account?” Mr. Lorry exclaimed, stepping forward. “My dear Charles, what can you mean? You have no accounts in France, other than those which are thankfully closed and settled.”

“I have one,” said Darnay, his gaze shifting to Doctor Manette, who had not spoken a word, but whose eyes had never left his face. “A debt of honour, long forgotten, but which has now been presented for payment.” He held out the letter, not to Lucie, not to Mr. Lorry, but to the Doctor. “It is from the servant of my family. A good and honest man named Gabelle. He was the local tax-collector, and steward of the estate. The estate of the Marquis St. Evrémonde.”

The name fell into the quiet room with the force of a stone dropped into a still pool. Lucie gasped and pressed her hand to her mouth. Mr. Lorry took a half-step back, his face a picture of dismay. But the effect upon Doctor Manette was the most terrible of all. The calm, collected physician vanished, and for a dreadful, fleeting moment, the shoemaker of the North Tower looked out from his eyes. His hand went to his temple in the old, bewildered gesture, and a grey pallor overspread his features, the very hue of the Bastille’s ancient stones. He did not take the letter. He stared at his son-in-law, his expression a maelstrom of confusion, ancient horror, and a dawning, dreadful comprehension.

“Evrémonde,” he whispered, the name a dry rustle in his throat.

“The name I renounced,” Charles said, with a quiet desperation. “The name and the inheritance I cast off on the day I first left that accursed land. But it seems it will not cast me off. This man, Gabelle, has been arrested. He is imprisoned in the Abbaye in Paris. He writes to me, the afor-named heir, to come and bear witness to his innocence, to speak for him. He says that my testimony is the only thing that can save him from the guillotine. He appeals to me, in the name of honour and of God, to come to his aid.”

“To go to Paris?” Mr. Lorry’s voice was incredulous, horrified. “To go into the very heart of the furnace? It is madness! Utter madness! No man’s life is safe there, least of all that of an emigrant, an aristocrat!”

“I am no aristocrat,” Charles countered, though his voice lacked its usual conviction. “I am a citizen of this country, a tutor of French, a man who has earned his own bread.”

“You were born an Evrémonde!” Mr. Lorry insisted, his agitation making him bolder than was his wont. “That is a stain that their new laws will not wash away; it is a crime for which there is no trial, only a verdict! To go there now is to put your head, willingly, into the mouth of the lion. No, into the jaws of the tiger! You must not! For Lucie’s sake, for the sake of all of us, you cannot go.”

All this time, Lucie had been watching her father. She saw the struggle within him; the shudder of his old agony warring with the new love that had remade his life. He seemed to be wrestling with a ghost, and she feared, for one heart-stopping moment, that the ghost would win, that he would relapse into the darkness from which she had rescued him. But then, as she watched, a change came over him. The look of vacant horror receded, and in its place came a new expression; one of resolute strength, of a sorrowful but unyielding purpose. The prisoner was gone. The physician had returned, and more than the physician, the father.

He straightened his shoulders and looked directly at Charles. His voice, when he finally spoke, was low, but as steady as a rock.

“What does the letter say?” he asked.

Charles, relieved beyond measure to hear his father-in-law’s sane and rational tone, began to read from the crumpled paper. He read of Gabelle’s terror, of the injustice of his arrest, of his pathetic faith that the young heir, so different from his wicked ancestors, would come and save him. He read the final, desperate plea: “For the love of Heaven, of justice, of generosity, of the honour of your noble name, I supplicate you, Monsieur heretofore the Marquis, to return and release me.”

When he had finished, the silence returned, heavier than before.

“He calls upon your honour,” the Doctor said, more to himself than to the others. He looked at Charles, and his gaze was filled with an almost unbearable sadness. He, more than any man alive, knew the price of a French prison. He knew the horrors that awaited any who fell into the hands of the self-proclaimed arbiters of justice. And yet, he also saw the man before him; the husband of his daughter, a man bound by a code of conduct that, in this new and brutal age, seemed a form of noble suicide.

“It is a trap,” said Miss Pross, speaking for the first time since the letter had been opened. Her voice was flat and hard. “They want you, not this Gabelle. They want an Evrémonde, and he is the bait. My Ladybird,” she said, turning to Lucie with a fierce and sudden tenderness, “do not let him go. Forbid it.”

Lucie turned her white face, streaming with silent tears, from her husband to her father. She was torn between the two poles of her existence: her wifely devotion and her daughterly fear. She saw the fatalistic resolve in Charles’s eyes, and she saw the profound, comprehending sorrow in her father’s.

“I cannot forbid him,” she said, her voice a mere thread of sound, “if his honour commands it. But Charles, my dearest, my husband, is there no other way? Can you not write? Can Mr. Lorry not use the influence of Tellson’s? Must it be you, and you alone?”

“It must,” said Charles, and he took her hands, his own cold as ice. “To send another would be an act of cowardice. It is my name, my family’s legacy, that has put him in this jeopardy. I, and I alone, can answer for it. I do not go as an Evrémonde. I go as Charles Darnay, a man of goodwill, to testify for an innocent servant. They are building a new Republic, founded on reason and justice. Surely they will listen to reason. They will see that I am no enemy.”

“They will see a title, a chateau, and a history of oppression,” Mr. Lorry retorted grimly. “And they will see nothing else. Think, Charles, think! The mail-coach to Dover, all those years ago. The message to my Lucie: ‘Recalled to Life.’ Are you now to travel that same road, in the opposite direction, to be recalled to death?”

The parallel was so stark, so dreadful, that it silenced even him. He looked at the Doctor, who stood with his hand on his daughter’s shoulder, a silent pillar of support.

“I must go,” Charles repeated, his voice now devoid of all argument, containing only the flat finality of a decision made. “I will be in no danger. I will travel quickly, bear my witness, and return before you have had time to miss me overmuch. The journey is short. A few weeks at most.”

A few weeks. The words hung in the air, a mockery of the eternity of dread they contained. A few weeks in a country where time was now measured by the fall of the blade, where each sunset brought a new list of the condemned.

The Doctor looked from his daughter’s weeping face to his son-in-law’s determined one. He, who had lost eighteen years of his life in a nameless tomb, understood the tyranny of a name, and the terrible power of the past. He saw that Charles was bound to this course, not by chains of iron, but by the far stronger, invisible chains of his own conscience. To argue further was useless.

“If you must go, Charles,” he said, and his voice held the authority of a man who had faced the worst of the world and survived, “then you will not go alone.”

A spark of hope flared in Lucie’s eyes. “Father! You will go with him?”

“No,” said the Doctor, gently stroking her hair. “That would be to invite disaster for us both. My history is too well known there, and too dangerous. No, I mean that we,” and he looked pointedly at Mr. Lorry, “will follow. We will provide you with a safe haven, a line of retreat. Mr. Lorry will establish a branch of Tellson’s in Paris, will he not? A place of business is a place of some neutrality. I will join him there. We will be your anchor in the storm.”

Mr. Lorry, who had been about to protest this wild scheme, found his objections dying on his lips. The quiet determination in the Doctor’s eyes was absolute. It was the look of a man who, having been saved, now saw his own chance to become a saviour. The business of Tellson’s Bank, which for so many years had been his whole world, suddenly seemed a small thing compared to the business of saving this family.

“Yes,” he said, his voice husky. “Yes, Doctor. We will establish a Paris branch. We will be there.”

And so, in the small, sunlit room that had so recently been the scene of domestic bliss, the desperate, impossible plan was laid. Charles was to depart that very night, travelling light and fast for Dover. He would carry papers identifying him as a French citizen returning to his homeland, a teacher of language residing in England. Mr. Lorry and the Doctor would follow in a few days, once the necessary arrangements for the bank could be made. Lucie, to her anguish and despair, was to remain in London with her child and Miss Pross, a waiting, praying sentinel.

The rest of the day passed in a dream of suppressed terror. A terrible, false calm descended, the kind that precedes a duel or an execution. A small bag was packed. Letters of credit were arranged by Mr. Lorry. Instructions were given and received in low tones, as if a loud word might shatter the fragile composure they had all constructed.

As evening drew in, casting long shadows that seemed to claw at the house from the street, the time came for him to leave. He stood in the hallway, holding Lucie in his arms. He kissed her tears away, murmuring words of love and reassurance that sounded hollow even to his own ears.

“It is but for a little while, my love,” he whispered into her golden hair. “I will write. I will be safe. Trust in me.”

“I trust you,” she sobbed, clinging to him. “It is them I do not trust. O, Charles, I have a terrible feeling that I am sending you away into a great darkness from which you will not return.”

He held her at arm’s length, and for a moment, he let his own mask of composure fall. She saw in his eyes a love so profound and a sorrow so deep that it mirrored her own. It was the look of a man who knew he was walking into his grave, but who walked with his head held high.

He turned to the Doctor. “Take care of her,” he said, his voice thick with unshed tears.

“With my life,” the Doctor replied, and he embraced Charles, not as a son-in-law, but as a son; a beloved, foolish, honourable son, marching off to a battle he could not possibly win.

Mr. Lorry shook his hand, a prolonged, firm grip that conveyed all the fears and hopes that a man of business could not put into words. Miss Pross stood stiffly by the door, her face a thundercloud of disapproval, but as he passed, she seized his hand and pressed it fiercely. “Come back to my Ladybird,” she commanded, her voice a harsh croak. “You had better.”

And then he was gone. The sound of the coach wheels receding down the quiet street was the only sound. They stood in the doorway, the three of them, a small, desolate group, listening until the sound faded into nothing. The house behind them, once a sanctuary of light and love, felt suddenly vast, cold, and empty. The ledger, which had been so joyfully balanced on the wedding-day, was indeed open again; and Charles Darnay had gone to France, a solitary figure on a dark road, to offer his own life as payment for a debt that was not his own. The gathering storm had broken, and its first victim was on his way to the guillotine.
